text: Owner decision 2026-07-21: the logical-map Artifact mirror (claude.ai/code/artifact/f20dda86-f0ac-4dba-b2a1-a191e6c3b034) is RETIRED — never republish it after map changes. Fully redundant with the permanent public Pages URL, and each republish costs an unavoidable web permission prompt (claude.ai web sessions apply no permission allowlists). The map's only maintained home is docs/site/logical-map.html served via Pages.

Owner decision 2026-07-21: docs/site/repo-map.html (physical-folders view) is deleted; docs/site/logical-map.html is the repo's single map. The add-a-file inventory drill now touches ONE map (SELF frame counts + Σ), CLAUDE.md layout table, and this file. Legacy stub docs/repo-map.html redirects to the logical map.

GitHub REST and GraphQL are separate quota pools drawn by every session on the account. Merging is REST; leaving draft is GraphQL-only, so a GraphQL-exhausted session can merge a non-draft PR but not un-draft one. Un-draft as soon as CI is green. Diagnose from the failing verb, and treat a throttle as retryable, never as a broken repo.

A UI suite written from the implementation confirms the implementation. Name the observable outcome first, then assert against it: 'the legend opens', not 'the handler fires'. Proven 2026-08-01 on this repo's map, where a 27-assertion Playwright gate stayed green through four interaction bugs a human found in minutes.

REJECTED: changing the PR-draft default to open ready-for-review. Raised after an exhausted GraphQL pool stalled three green PRs at un-draft. The cause was session volume, not the draft policy, and git.md's existing mitigation already covers it — un-draft as soon as CI goes green. Opening ready-for-review stays a per-PR judgement when already quota-strained.

Creating a PR subscribes the session to its activity harness-side; no tool call is involved and omitting one prevents nothing. subscribe_pr_activity exists to take over a PR the session did not open, or to re-subscribe after unsubscribing. The only lever on your own PR is unsubscribe_pr_activity after the fact.

A skipped-test CI gate cannot key on whether a skip carries a reason string: every shipped test.skip has one, including the fixture-absence skips it must catch. Key an allowlist by stable test identity — project, spec file, full test title — checked against a JSON reporter run, so intended skips are enumerated once and any new skip fails.

One shared environment serves every repo, and its cached image keeps whatever plugins the installer once installed. Re-saving the Setup script does not reliably rebuild it. So an installer fix reaches only repos that commit .claude/hooks/session-start.sh. Symptom: one repo spews a plugin error while claude.directives is clean — the difference is the hook, not the environment.

A Python str.replace() whose needle does not match returns the string unchanged and raises nothing. A scripted fix silently no-oped and the commit message then claimed a change the file never received. Assert every scripted edit applied (assert s.count(a)==1 before replacing), and verify claims against the file as written.

A validator has two surfaces needing OPPOSITE treatment: accepted VALUES allowlisted, DETECTION exhaustive and fail-closed. Narrowing detection silently skips input — how check-landing-cards.js broke. But exhaustiveness has a cost ceiling: there the owner ruled six residual gaps acceptable (2026-08-22) rather than add a parser dependency. Aim for it; never reopen a ruled limit.

A GitHub ruleset bypass entry exempts an ACTOR, not a workflow or a token. Bypassing the account that owns a PAT exempts every push that account makes — sessions included — while the ruleset still reads Active. Recall whenever a scheduled workflow's direct push collides with branch protection: delete the workflow, never widen the bypass.

Changing a rule in one file leaves every file that ACTS on it stating the opposite. Re-confirmed three times inside one PR (#266): the exported directive, then the bootstrap scaffold, then four docs still demanding a now-unused secret. After any rule change grep case-INSENSITIVELY for every name involved, and fix the consumers in the same commit.

Session clones are SHALLOW by default, so git log answers history questions from a truncated window with no error — a 16-day view returned a confident "active" to a 60-day threshold downstream. Before any claim from log depth (age, gaps, last-touched, authorship): git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository, then git fetch --unshallow. Bare --deepen exits 129, and --deepen N can still land short of the cutoff.

Two sessions can drive one PR at once. Before acting on a PR you did not open, check it is not still moving: compare updated_at and newest commit time against now, and read existing comments. A flagged label with unresolved threads is often a session mid-iteration, not an abandoned PR; duplicating its Codex re-request spends the account-wide weekly pool.

An unratified company-wide rule is self-consistent, so a consistency audit never flags it. The provenance pass has TWO failure modes: it fires on a section that merely defers to a stamped ruling, and it can be talked out of a real finding by an entailment argued from a ruling that does not actually reach that far (design.md's token mechanism, caught by Codex 2026-08-22). Deference must be cited, never constructed.

Probe a default-branch protection rule through the GitHub contents API (create_or_update_file, branch=main), never git push: a remote session's push scope covers only its designated branch, so a push to main returns a sandbox 403 indistinguishable from the rule working. Use a fresh probe filename each attempt.

A plain push does NOT re-trigger Codex. Its only triggers are opening a PR for review, marking a draft ready, and an explicit '@codex review' comment. Silence after a push means never asked, not unavailable — do not take git.md's documented-unavailable path on a head that was only pushed. Measured 2026-08-23: an explicit request drew a review in 4-7 minutes every time.

codex-monitor clears codex-flagged for the SHA it reviewed and cannot un-clear on a later push, so an absent label may describe a superseded head. The label is weaker evidence than git.md's gate, which wants a Codex response naming the CURRENT head. Check commit_id, not the label — #283 would otherwise have merged its most substantive change unreviewed.

Three times in one session a rule landed in a file its actor never opens: an owner-wide delivery rule in internal learnings, a session instruction in a runbook /refresh-repo never reads, and a fleet ruling in referenced docs while the inherited directives went untouched. Before writing a rule, name who executes it and confirm they read that file.

Never judge Codex from the codex-flagged label: absence proves nothing, presence blocks. The embedded reaction summary (issue_read->get) has no author or timestamp; the reaction LIST endpoint has both but was unreachable from a remote session (2026-08-23). Ordering (push->request->reaction) is necessary, NOT sufficient — an earlier in-flight request's reaction satisfies it while describing the old SHA. Never clear the gate silently.

When a signal carries no identifier, no amount of timestamp comparison recovers one. Correlate by identity or stop claiming correlation. (Codex's 👍 carries no SHA; asking Codex a direct SHA-naming question yields an authored comment instead — UNTESTED as of 2026-08-23, per directives/git.md.)

Sweep for the CLAIM, not the wording — the second copy never uses the first copy's words. Three traps: a file you JUST edited is not thereby swept; the CANONICAL file is also a consumer of itself, and the short distance hides the contradiction; a correction in learnings.jsonl must reuse the key, since a new key supersedes nothing.

A single conflict-resolution rule applied across a stacked cherry-pick is how a clean queue produces a broken tree. THREE kinds, and the correct move differs for each: a GENERATED file is regenerated from its source, never merged; a PROSE LIST (workflow steps, CLAUDE.md's local gate, directive bullets) takes the UNION, because both sides are additions at one anchor; CODE takes neither. Rehearse on a throwaway branch and re-verify the delicate file after EVERY step with ITS format's verifier (node --check for JS, a parse for YAML, a rebuild for a generated file), because the break is silent until something reads it. Detail: #313.

Writing that a value is now shared does not share it. If two places must agree, make one of them a REFERENCE the other expands at compile time, or a checker that compares them. Prose in a commit message is not a mechanism, and a fix whose only enforcement is the author's memory is the defect it replaced. Trigger: committing the same string in two places. Detail: #313.

Deriving test cases from a definition and hand-writing them fail in OPPOSITE directions, so a suite that matters needs both. DERIVED cases catch DRIFT but never NARROWING — deleting an entry from the definition deletes its probe in the same edit and the suite stays green. LITERAL cases catch narrowing precisely because they name the value. A test that passes with AND without the thing it tests has measured nothing. Detail: #313.

Cross-session messaging can SILENTLY not deliver, and fire_trigger's return says whether it did: the target's id carries the target's id with its prefix SWAPPED, not appended -- session_01ABC returns cse_01ABC, not cse_session_01ABC. When it did not deliver, the value is an unrelated cse_ id and a fresh session ran the prompt instead. Measured 2026-08-26 across four sends. PERFECTLY CORRELATED in those four with passing the optional `text` parameter to fire_trigger. Treat text as suspect until retested, and always compare the returned session_id against the target before assuming delivery. Note a poke-only trigger never fires on its own, so an unfired one sits inert rather than arriving later -- it is a lost message, not a delayed one.

A check INSIDE the thing it verifies cannot report a failure where that thing never ran, OR failed BEFORE REACHING it: either way those steps did not execute, so the failure is SILENT. A workflow_run watcher on types:[completed] fires only on a TERMINAL state, so a hang is covered by NEITHER. An arm buys a RUN at the right moment, not detection. Add, repoint or remove is a multi-branch table: READ automations.md W1-W3, never from here (#368).

A RETRY watcher is not symmetric with a MONITOR: it re-runs the whole watched run, so a retry arm replays the project's entire build where a monitor only observes. That COST, not a prohibition, is why their rules differ. W3 has an exception and a revisit trigger; paraphrasing it here dropped the exception, so READ automations.md W3. Trigger: editing a retry watcher — ask what a fire costs.

Do not assert about an artifact you have not read — but the fix is USUALLY TO GO READ IT, not to ask. ACT scope and READ scope are different things: the GitHub MCP can only WRITE against this session's repos, while ANY PUBLIC REPO IS ALWAYS READABLE via raw.githubusercontent.com, api.github.com or the codeload tarball, with no MCP, no gh and no clone -- /do-repo packages exactly this. Then fetch if you can, and ask only when the repo is genuinely private or otherwise unreachable -- and say WHICH of those two it is, because 'I can't see it' and 'I didn't look' are different admissions.

A rule written as "X only on A" is a ONE-SIDED sentence: the B case is implicit, so anything that belongs in it — most often a documented exception — has nowhere to live and quietly disappears. Two explicit branches make an omitted exception a VISIBLY EMPTY BRANCH rather than an absent sentence. When the same correction lands three times, stop fixing instances and change the FORM: fixing site five of a six-site error guarantees site seven exists. Detail: #317.

Ask of any guard: what does it look like when it FAILS? If that is indistinguishable from success, it is broken — but only where failure must stop progress. Deliberate fail-open speed bumps (push-gate, wait-gate) are correct. Shapes: a default meaning off (timeout 0), a broad catch eating a ReferenceError, a skip rendering green. Instances and detection: directives#323.

Bound a rule by what is ALLOWED, not by enumerating what is forbidden — an enumeration leaves a case outside, and a reviewer finds it. A shared-tree exception listing forbidden git commands missed add and commit; the replacement is a capability boundary whose complement needs no list. Test for this shape: if the rule says "except X, Y, Z", ask what W is — if you cannot prove the list is closed, state the allowed capability instead. Detail: #362.

When three attempts to state a rule PRECISELY each leave a case outside, stop claiming closure and say the list is examples. An incomplete list of EXAMPLES costs nothing, while an incomplete list of REQUIREMENTS is an exemption — the load-bearing line being that a case absent from the list is NOT thereby exempt. The distinguishing question: does the rule need a CLOSED set to be sound? If yes and you cannot close it, it is a disposition. Detail: #362.

A turn-end rule cannot bind a session to report work it had to DISCOVER: it authors both the answer and the candidate set. Four wordings failed — the first judged a correct waiting turn defective, the rest were satisfied on their own terms. Keep the triggers, drop the test. An externally fixed expectation is a different case, on conditions not stated here. Detail: #362, #363, #368.

When a regex's exclusion list grows to approximate a boundary the FORMAT already defines, move structural recognition out of the regex — parse the format, or normalise before matching. Not a rule about open inputs generally: parsers and capability boundaries handle those with a positive grammar. Trigger: writing a second 'must not cross X'. Detail in #365, #367.

A disposition nothing can reach reads as care and adds none. An OUT OF SCOPE branch was unreachable because the scope gate already defined candidates as authorized work only, making a three-way partition a two-way one with a decoy. Trigger: adding an 'other' or 'neither' case — ask what input lands there. Detail in #362.
